conceptTag: Xerox studies what top sellers do
readerTitle: What Xerox learned by watching its best sellers
caseNote: 실제 기업·연구 (Xerox가 후원한 Neil Rackham·Huthwaite의 영업 통화 연구) + 가상 적용 (난방 수리, 식자재 유통)
insight: 큰 거래에서 뛰어난 영업자는 해결책을 밀어붙이지 않는다. 고객이 스스로 문제의 크기를 가늠하도록 돕는다.
misconception: 최고의 영업자는 말을 잘하고 클로징을 잘하는 사람이다. 작은 거래에서 통하는 방법은 큰 거래에서도 통한다.

sources.text: Rackham, N. (1988). SPIN Selling. McGraw-Hill. (35,000건 이상의 영업 통화 연구, 클로징 기법의 효과, 네 가지 질문 유형)
Rackham, N. (1989). Major Account Sales Strategy. McGraw-Hill.
Huthwaite International, company history (연구 수행 기관, 후원 기업)

factChecks.note: "약 12년간 35,000건 이상의 영업 통화"는 SPIN Selling 서문과 각종 요약에 반복해서 나오는 수치입니다. 원문에서 기간과 건수를 다시 확인하세요.
Xerox가 연구를 후원한 기업 중 하나였다는 점은 Rackham 본인 서술과 Huthwaite 자료에 나옵니다. 후원 범위와 Xerox가 결과를 교육에 어떻게 반영했는지는 세부 내용을 지어내지 않고 일반적으로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 확인 필요.
연구 시작 시점은 1970년대로 자주 서술됩니다. 카드에는 "In the 1970s"로만 적었습니다. 정확한 연도는 원문을 확인하세요.
"클로징 기법은 작은 거래에서는 효과가 있었지만 큰 거래에서는 오히려 성과를 떨어뜨렸다", "성과가 낮은 영업자는 상황 질문을 많이 했다"는 결론은 SPIN Selling 2~3장에 나옵니다. 구체적 비율은 쓰지 않았습니다.
8번 카드의 4% 가격 차이는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: What Xerox learned by watching its best sellers
body: In the 1970s, a research team began sitting in on sales calls. These weren't role-plays. They were real meetings with real buyers.

Over about 12 years, Neil Rackham's team at the firm Huthwaite studied more than 35,000 calls. Xerox was among the companies backing the work. The question was simple: in big, expensive deals, what do the best sellers actually do differently?

image.label: An observer taking notes during a sales meeting
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 회의실 테이블에서 영업자와 고객이 대화하고, 구석에 클립보드를 든 관찰자가 조용히 기록 중. 1970~80년대 사무실 분위기(복사기, 서류철). 실제 회사 로고나 제품 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Place your bet.
body: Xerox sold costly copiers and office systems to companies. Buyers often took weeks or months to decide, and several people had a say.
Which habit do you think best separated the top sellers in these big deals?

options.text: They used proven closing techniques and asked for the order early and often
options.feedback: This is what much sales training taught. The study found closing helped in small, quick sales but tended to hurt in big ones, where buyers felt pushed.

options.text: They explained more product features and how each one could help
options.feedback: Product knowledge matters. But pitching before the buyer felt a real need often invited objections, especially about price.

options.text: They asked questions that helped the buyer see what a problem was costing them
options.feedback: Yes. The buyer ends up making the case for change in their own words. The next cards show how.

cards.title: The classic playbook broke in big deals.
body: The researchers found that standard techniques worked in small sales. For a cheap item bought in one meeting, a firm push to close could lift results.
In large sales, the same push tended to lower them. A buyer who must defend a big spend to colleagues doesn't want to be rushed.
Top sellers spent their time differently. They asked more questions, and one kind of question stood out.

cards.title: Implication questions
body: **Implication questions** ask what a problem leads to: the costs, delays and knock-on effects.
A buyer admits the copier jams. That sounds small. But what happens when it jams the night before a bid is due? Who stays late? What does a missed deadline cost?
Weaker sellers heard the problem and jumped to the pitch. Top sellers stayed with it until the buyer saw a problem bigger than the price.

image.label: A small problem growing into a chain of consequences
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 작은 아이콘 "Copier jams", 화살표를 따라 점점 커지는 아이콘 "Late bid", "Overtime", "Lost contract". 마지막 아이콘 옆에 작은 가격표를 두어 문제가 가격보다 커진 느낌을 줌. 실제 제품 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four kinds of questions
body: Rackham grouped sellers' questions into four types. Their first letters spell **SPIN**.

breakdown.label: Situation
breakdown.detail: Facts about the buyer today. Needed, but buyers find too many dull

breakdown.label: Implication
breakdown.detail: What the problem leads to, and what it costs

breakdown.label: Need-payoff
breakdown.detail: What solving it would be worth, in the buyer's words

cards.callout: Less successful sellers leaned on Situation questions. Top sellers asked far more of the last two.
cards.softwareNote: A prospect says onboarding new staff is slow. Asking how many hires are planned and what a slow first month costs turns a nice-to-have tool into a budget line.

cards.title: A heating repair, not a quote.
body: A homeowner calls about a noisy boiler. The contractor could quote a replacement on the spot.
Instead she asks: How often has it cut out this winter? What happened last time? Did anyone take a day off waiting for repairs? Is anyone at home who struggles in the cold?
Now the homeowner is describing why a reliable system matters. The quote lands on a problem the buyer has already sized.

image.label: A contractor listening to a homeowner by a boiler
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 작업복 차림의 기술자가 공구를 내려놓고 메모하며 집주인의 이야기를 듣는 장면. 배경에 보일러와 담요를 두른 가족. 견적서는 아직 접힌 채 주머니에. 상표 없음.

cards.title: Questions aren't a trick.
body: Implication questions work when the problem is real. Used to inflate a minor issue, they feel like manipulation, and buyers notice.
They also take time. For a quick, low-cost purchase, a short helpful answer can beat a long interview.
Keep the source in mind too. The research came from a firm that sold sales training, and it shows what top sellers did. It doesn't prove each habit caused their success.

cards.title: Now you're a food distributor.
body: You're meeting the buyer for a group of five restaurants. She mentions their current supplier's deliveries sometimes arrive late. Your trucks are more reliable, but you cost about 4% more.
What's your next move?

options.text: Lead with your on-time record and offer to match their current price
options.feedback: You may win the account, but you give away margin before learning whether late deliveries cost her more than 4%.

options.text: Ask what happens in the kitchens when a delivery is late, and how often it happens
options.feedback: If late produce means menu items run out on a busy night, she'll weigh that against 4% herself. If it barely matters, you've learned that cheaply.

options.text: Note it, then email a full price list and brochure after the meeting
options.feedback: Polite and low-pressure, but the brochure competes on price alone. The problem she raised goes unexplored.

cards.title: In big sales, help the buyer size the problem before you offer the fix.
body: Closing harder rarely wins large deals. Questions about consequences let the buyer see why change is worth the price.
**Try it today:** before your next important customer conversation, write down one problem they likely have and three questions about what it leads to: cost, time and people.
